def: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is an oscillatory motion in which the restoring acceleration is always directly proportional to the displacement and directed opposite to it.
points: Restoring force F = -kx, so acceleration a = -(k/m)x = -ω²x, where ω² = k/m.
This gives the SHM differential equation: d²x/dt² = -ω²x.
The negative sign shows the acceleration always points back toward the mean (equilibrium) position.
The general solution of this equation is x = A sin(ωt + φ), where A is amplitude and φ is initial phase.
ω is called angular frequency, related to period by ω = 2π/T.
Any motion satisfying this differential equation is, by definition, SHM — this is used to identify SHM in problems.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Displacement x from mean position"] --> B["Restoring force F = -kx"]
  B --> C["Acceleration a = -omega squared x"]
  C --> D["Body accelerates back to mean position"]
  D --> A

example: A particle has acceleration a = -16x (SI units). Comparing with a = -ω²x, ω² = 16, so ω = 4 rad/s, and T = 2π/4 = 1.57 s.
tip: To prove a motion is SHM, show F or a is proportional to -x; just saying 'it oscillates' is not enough for full marks.

t: Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration in SHM
def: In SHM, displacement, velocity and acceleration all vary sinusoidally with time but have different phases relative to each other.
points: Displacement: x = A sin(ωt), where A is amplitude.
Velocity: v = dx/dt = Aω cos(ωt), which can also be written as v = ω√(A² − x²).
Acceleration: a = dv/dt = -Aω² sin(ωt) = -ω²x.
Velocity is maximum (= Aω) at the mean position (x = 0) and zero at extreme positions (x = ±A).
Acceleration is zero at the mean position and maximum (= Aω²) at the extreme positions.
Velocity leads displacement by 90°, and acceleration leads velocity by 90° (or is 180° out of phase with displacement).
formula: x = A sin(ωt)   v = ω√(A² − x²)   a = -ω²x

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["At mean position x=0"] --> B["v is maximum, a is zero"]
  C["At extreme position x=A"] --> D["v is zero, a is maximum"]

tip: Remember the two extreme cases: v is max & a is zero at mean position; v is zero & a is max at extreme position — asked almost every year.

def: A particle in SHM continuously exchanges energy between kinetic and potential forms, but the total mechanical energy remains constant.
points: Kinetic energy: KE = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)mω²(A² − x²), maximum at mean position.
Potential energy: PE = (1/2)kx² = (1/2)mω²x², maximum at extreme positions.
Total energy: E = KE + PE = (1/2)mω²A², which stays constant throughout the motion.
At the mean position (x=0), all energy is kinetic; at extreme positions (x=±A), all energy is potential.
The total energy depends on amplitude squared — doubling amplitude quadruples total energy.
This conservation follows directly from the fact that the restoring force is conservative.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["At mean position"] --> B["KE = maximum, PE = zero"]
  C["At extreme position"] --> D["KE = zero, PE = maximum"]
  B --> E["Total energy E constant throughout"]
  D --> E

example: m = 0.5 kg, ω = 4 rad/s, A = 0.2 m: E = (1/2) x 0.5 x 16 x 0.04 = 0.16 J (constant at every point of oscillation).
tip: Draw/describe how KE and PE graphs (vs displacement x) are parabolas that add up to a constant horizontal line — a good diagram-based answer.

def: A simple pendulum and a mass-spring system are two common mechanical examples of SHM, each with its own period formula based on its restoring force.
points: A simple pendulum is a point mass suspended from a light, inextensible string, oscillating with small angular displacement.
For small angles, the restoring force component is -mg sinθ ≈ -mgθ, giving SHM with period T = 2π√(L/g).
The period of a simple pendulum does not depend on mass, only on length L and gravity g.
A mass-spring system has restoring force F = -kx (Hooke's law), giving period T = 2π√(m/k).
Here k is the spring's force constant (stiffness); stiffer springs (larger k) give shorter period (faster oscillation).
Both systems are SHM because their equations of motion reduce to d²x/dt² = -ω²x.

diagram.draw: Draw two setups side by side. Left: a pendulum — a string of length L fixed at top, with a bob at the bottom shown displaced through small angle θ from the vertical, restoring force arrow shown. Right: a mass hanging from a vertical spring of constant k, displaced by x from equilibrium, with restoring force arrow pointing back toward equilibrium.

example: A pendulum of length 1 m on Earth (g=9.8): T = 2π sqrt(1/9.8) = 2π x 0.319 = 2.01 s.
tip: State clearly that pendulum period is independent of mass and amplitude (for small angles) — this is a frequently asked conceptual point.

def: Phase describes the state (position and direction of motion) of a particle in SHM at any instant, while epoch is the initial phase angle at time t = 0.
points: In x = A sin(ωt + φ), the quantity (ωt + φ) is called the phase at time t.
Phase tells us both where the particle is in its cycle and which direction it is moving.
Epoch (φ) is the value of phase at t = 0, i.e., the starting condition of the motion.
If φ = 0, the particle starts from the mean position moving in positive direction.
If φ = π/2, the particle starts from the extreme position (x = A) with zero velocity.
Two particles with the same ω but different φ are said to have a phase difference, which determines how 'out of step' they are.
formula: Phase = ωt + φ     Epoch = φ (value of phase at t = 0)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["phi = 0"] --> B["starts at mean position"]
  C["phi = pi over 2"] --> D["starts at extreme position"]
  B --> E["Phase = omega t + phi tracks motion over time"]
  D --> E

example: If x = 0.05 sin(10t + π/2), epoch = π/2 rad, meaning the particle starts at its extreme position x = 0.05 m at t = 0.
tip: Phase difference between two SHMs of π means they are exactly out of step (one at max when other is at min) — useful for comparing two oscillators.

def: Damped oscillations lose energy and amplitude over time due to resistive (friction/drag) forces. Forced oscillations are driven by an external periodic force, and resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude.
points: In damped SHM, a resistive force (like air drag) removes energy each cycle, so amplitude decreases exponentially with time.
Damped oscillations can be underdamped (oscillates with decreasing amplitude), critically damped, or overdamped (no oscillation, returns slowly).
Forced oscillation happens when an external periodic driving force is continuously applied to a system, replacing lost energy.
The system eventually oscillates at the driving frequency, not necessarily its own natural frequency.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency, producing very large amplitude.
Examples: pushing a swing at its natural rhythm (resonance), shock absorbers in cars (damping) to quickly kill unwanted oscillations.
formula: At resonance: driving frequency = natural frequency → amplitude is maximum

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Driving frequency far from natural frequency"] --> B["Small amplitude"]
  C["Driving frequency equals natural frequency"] --> D["Resonance: amplitude is maximum"]

example: Soldiers marching in step across a bridge at a frequency matching the bridge's natural frequency can cause resonance and dangerous large oscillations — hence the command to break step on bridges.
tip: Give one damping example (shock absorber) and one resonance example (swing or bridge) — examiners look for real-life application, not just definitions.
